extracted.intended_audience: European patent attorneys, patent applicants, opponents, and EPO appeals practitioners
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and evaluative criteria for presenting cases, admitting amendments, and drafting/defending European patent applications and related IP filings before the EPO (appeals, sufficiency, added‑matter, clarity, trademarks, UPC opt-outs).

rubrics_metrics.name: Statement(s) of grounds of appeal form the basis of proceedings (Art. 12(1) RPBA)
rubrics_metrics.description: The statement(s) of grounds of appeal and any replies thereto form the basis of the appeal proceedings.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Any request or statement a party made during first instance proceedings that is not expressly incorporated in the statement of grounds of appeal or the reply may not form part of the appeal. When preparing an appeal or reply, parties should expressly incorporate any first‑instance elements they wish to maintain unless consciously abandoned. Mere references to first‑instance submissions are generally insufficient. (See Art. 12(1) RPBA and accompanying commentary.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Complete appeal case must be contained in grounds/reply (Art. 12(3) RPBA)
rubrics_metrics.description: “The statement of grounds of appeal and the reply shall contain a party‘s complete appeal case.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For patent proprietors: any auxiliary request maintained on appeal must be substantiated in the statement of grounds or reply, even if not decided in first instance. For opponents: all objections against all auxiliary requests on file must be submitted at this initial stage rather than waiting for the Board. Failure to present a complete case risks inadmissibility or a Board allowing an un‑objected request.

rubrics_metrics.name: Incorporate first-instance elements expressly or risk abandonment
rubrics_metrics.description: Any element presented in the first instance proceedings must be expressly incorporated into the statement of grounds of appeal or the reply if it is to form part of the appeal; otherwise it may be treated as abandoned.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If an element was presented but not maintained during first instance and then reintroduced on appeal, it has very little chance of being admitted except in unusual circumstances (Art.12(6) RPBA). Parties should consider filing any requests, facts, objections, or evidence during first instance if they were in a position to do so.

rubrics_metrics.name: Opponents must timely raise objections to auxiliary requests
rubrics_metrics.description: Opponents must submit all objections against all auxiliary requests on file at the initial stage of the appeal.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Relying on possible remittal or awaiting the Board may be risky: in absence of timely objections a Board may allow an auxiliary request because no objections are on file.

rubrics_metrics.name: What constitutes a case amendment
rubrics_metrics.description: A case amendment may be a new line of argumentation, new evidence, new claim amendments, or even reference to a new passage in a document already on file.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognise that amendments are broadly defined; examples and case references show that adding arguments/evidence/claim variants or pointing to previously unrelied parts of documents can be treated as amendments (see J 14/19 and other cited decisions).

rubrics_metrics.name: Admission of amendments filed with the grounds of appeal (Art. 12(4) RPBA)
rubrics_metrics.description: If a case amendment is made with the grounds of appeal or response thereto, such an amendment is admitted only at the Board's discretion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The appellant must draw attention to each case amendment and provide reasons why it was submitted only in the appeal proceedings. This must be done proactively; failure to provide reasons may lead to rejection as inadmissible (see T 81/20, T 1456/20).

rubrics_metrics.name: Admissibility of later amendments — convergent three‑level approach (Art.12/13 RPBA)
rubrics_metrics.description: Admissibility of amendments is assessed under a convergent approach: first level Art.12(4) (amendments with grounds/reply), second level Art.13(1) (amendments after grounds/response), third level Art.13(2) (after summons to oral proceedings).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The restrictions are cumulative: an amendment must satisfy earlier levels as well as later ones. Boards apply increasingly strict criteria as proceedings advance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Factors for admitting post‑grounds amendments (Art.13(1) RPBA)
rubrics_metrics.description: Amendments filed after the grounds of appeal and response term are admitted only at the Board’s discretion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Significant factors include: (i) whether the amendment addresses new issues that were admissibly raised by another party or the Board, (ii) procedural economy considerations, and (iii) whether the amendment, prima facie, overcomes open issues and does not give rise to new objections. Empirical note: many Art.13(1) citations occur for amendments after summons and are frequently not admitted.

rubrics_metrics.name: Exceptional circumstances required after summons (Art.13(2) RPBA)
rubrics_metrics.description: Amendments made after the parties have been summoned to oral proceedings require “exceptional circumstances, which have been justified with cogent reasons” to be taken into account.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Art.13(2) is even more restrictive and also subjects the amendment to criteria of Art.12(4) and Art.13(1). Boards generally take a strong line: statistics reviewed showed only about 22% admission for late amendments in the sampled decisions; difference exists between ex parte and inter partes proceedings. A common accepted reason is amendment in response to a new point raised by the Board in its preliminary opinion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proactive disclosure of reasons for amendments
rubrics_metrics.description: The filing party must proactively draw attention to each amendment and provide reasons explaining why it was submitted only in the appeal proceedings.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do this even before any admissibility issue is suggested; failing to do so risks inadmissibility (see T 81/20).

rubrics_metrics.name: Situations that may not be considered a case amendment
rubrics_metrics.description: Certain actions may not amount to a 'case amendment'—for example, mere deletion of subject matter (e.g., deleting claims/options), correction of errors, or further elaboration of existing arguments (e.g., by references to further case law) in some circumstances.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Boards have found that deletions, corrections, and elaborations sometimes do not constitute amendments (see T 914/18, T 2167/17, T 2988/18), but whether they do is fact‑specific.

rubrics_metrics.name: Article 83 EPC — sufficiency standard
rubrics_metrics.description: A patent application must disclose the claimed invention sufficiently clearly and completely for it to be performed by the skilled person without undue burden, taking into account the common general knowledge.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Applicants should ensure the invention is described in enough detail to allow performance across the full scope of the claims. Opponents should file evidence showing serious doubts regarding performance. Sufficiency objections are more common in life sciences; supplementary technical information is restricted in opposition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Medical use claims — plausibility requirement
rubrics_metrics.description: For medical use claims that recite a therapeutic effect, it is necessary to establish that the claimed therapeutic effect can plausibly be achieved based on the application, the prior art and the common general knowledge.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Post‑filed experimental data cannot be the sole basis for compliance with Article 83 EPC. Boards have accepted plausibility where prior art/patent teaching made the effect plausible or where limited pre‑clinical data in the application supported plausibility (see T 0184/16, T 0966/18, T 2015/20). Absolute proof or clinical data are not always required.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of prior art and post‑filed data in plausibility
rubrics_metrics.description: Prior art teaching may be decisive in acknowledging plausibility; limited pre‑clinical or in vitro data in the application can render a therapeutic effect plausible.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Boards have distinguished sufficiency from inventive step — relying on prior art to support plausibility does not necessarily undermine inventive step. However, post‑filed data may be used as confirmation but not as sole basis (see cited Board decisions).

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition and disclosure of parameters
rubrics_metrics.description: Applications should contain a complete definition of any parameters appearing in claims, including methods for their determination, particularly for unconventional parameters.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Failure to define how to measure/determine a parameter can lead to insufficiency because the skilled person cannot perform the invention over the full scope (example T 1050/16 concerning crotch length measurement).

rubrics_metrics.name: Sufficiency assessment for mechanical inventions
rubrics_metrics.description: In mechanical fields the skilled person may be expected to identify and exclude non‑working embodiments (e.g., air inlets positioned so low that sea water enters), and Boards may apply different reasoning than in chemistry.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Opponents arguing insufficiency for mechanical inventions must show an impossible burden across the scope; Boards may accept that the skilled person would exclude obviously non‑working embodiments (see T 2773/18).

rubrics_metrics.name: Uncertainty from G 2/21 — standard for admitting post‑filed evidence
rubrics_metrics.description: Questions before the Enlarged Board in G 2/21 concern whether admittance of post‑filed evidence should be judged by ab initio plausibility (skilled person would have considered the effect plausible at filing) or ab initio implausibility (skilled person would have seen no reason to consider the effect implausible at filing).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Although posed in inventive‑step context, the issue is relevant for Article 83 assessments of claims reciting a technical effect (e.g., medical use claims). The Enlarged Board’s decision is expected to clarify admissibility standards.

rubrics_metrics.name: Gold standard for Art.123(2) EPC (added‑matter)
rubrics_metrics.description: Any amendment to a European patent application or patent must be directly and unambiguously derivable from the application as filed, taking common general knowledge into account (the EPO 'gold standard' from G 2/10).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is applied strictly: speculative or uncertain disclosures in the description are unlikely to provide a basis for post‑filing claim amendments. The application should ideally include concrete statements (e.g., dependent claims) that can serve as basis for later amendments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Speculative/hypothetical statements cannot support claim amendments (Art.123(2))
rubrics_metrics.description: Statements expressing expectation or hypothetical therapeutic effects (e.g., clinical trial outlines without results) are not direct and unambiguous disclosure for claiming the therapeutic effect.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example T 2842/18: an example stating 'it is expected that re‑treatment ... will be effective' was held to express uncertainty and could not be used to amend claims. Plausibility is irrelevant to the Art.123(2) assessment: direct and unambiguous disclosure is the criterion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinctive character for three‑dimensional trademarks in EU
rubrics_metrics.description: A three‑dimensional mark consisting of the shape of a product must significantly differ from the norms and customs of the relevant sector to have distinctive character.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Novelty/originality of the product shape is irrelevant to distinctive character; the norms and customs test must consider all shapes consumers are accustomed to seeing (not merely the statistically most common). If the shape would 'surprise' the relevant public and depart significantly from sector norms, it can indicate commercial origin (Guerlain v EUIPO, Case T‑488/20).

rubrics_metrics.name: Clarity requirement for claims (Art.84 EPC)
rubrics_metrics.description: The claims shall be clear and concise and be supported by the description.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Boards often raise clarity objections, sometimes encouraging incorporation of implementation details into claims. There is no single robust test; applicants often limit claims to avoid protracted examination. Clarity objections in Europe differ from national practices (e.g., Germany).

rubrics_metrics.name: Claim construction is not purely linguistic
rubrics_metrics.description: Claim construction is performed by the skilled person 'with a mind willing to understand' to arrive at a technically sensible interpretation rather than by excluding only illogical readings.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This pragmatic, technical approach affects how broad features are interpreted and whether further technical features are implied by claim wording (see T 0935/14).

rubrics_metrics.name: Technical consistency as a prerequisite for clarity
rubrics_metrics.description: Even if two features are individually clear, they must be consistent with each other from a technical point of view to yield a clear claim interpretation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If a literal reading would produce a technically inconsistent or unusable combination, the claim may be unclear.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguishing 'broad but clear' from 'broad and vague'
rubrics_metrics.description: A broad claim is not unclear per se; vagueness arises if the wording prevents an unambiguous distinction from the prior art or allows different but equally valid interpretations whose full scopes are not sufficiently disclosed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the 'border test': ask whether the borders of the scope of protection can be clearly inferred by the skilled person and whether further technical features are implied by the broad wording. If such implied features are unclear, the claim is vague (case T 0935/14).

rubrics_metrics.name: Minimal claim construction and implied features
rubrics_metrics.description: Assess whether a claim is technically consistent under a minimal construction without reading in further implied features; if minimal reading yields inconsistency, identify whether specific implied features are required and whether they are clear.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If it is not clear what implied further technical features precisely are, the claim is vague and thus not clear. The Board used this to invalidate overlapping 'account' definitions in T 0935/14.

rubrics_metrics.name: Plan for UPC opt‑out during preparatory phase
rubrics_metrics.description: Proprietors of European patents and pending applications should plan early if and how to use the UPC opt‑out mechanism, which will be available during a limited window near the end of the Preparatory Phase before the UPC opens.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Preparatory Committee expects roughly eight months’ preparatory phase; the last three months are the key window to opt out before rights can be locked in by a third‑party complaint. Proprietors should start planning early to opt out in an orderly fashion.
